justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple users through wide motor lanes, a planted median, and a separate sidewalk/corridor on the right side, suggesting a relatively orderly distribution of road space.

Accessibility is only moderate because no curb ramps, tactile paving, zebra crossings, or other barrier-free crossing details are visible from this view, so equal usability for all users cannot be confirmed.

Fairness is limited by the strong visual priority given to motor traffic: the roadway is wide and clearly marked, while dedicated cycling space is not visible and pedestrian space appears set back from the carriageway.
The continuous side path on the right appears smooth and unobstructed by parked cars, which supports general access for pedestrians and potentially other non-motorized users.
safety: Safety is supported by the broad roadway, clear lane markings, and low apparent traffic volume, which make vehicle movements more legible for all road users.
A planted median separates opposing directions of travel, reducing head-on conflict risk and helping organize traffic flow.
Streetlights are present along the corridor, which suggests some nighttime safety provision even though actual illumination cannot be judged in daytime.
Safety is constrained by relatively high design speed cues: long straight geometry, multiple wide lanes, and sparse friction from crossings or roadside activity may encourage faster driving.
No visible protected bike lane or marked pedestrian crossing is present in the scene, leaving uncertainty about conflict protection for cyclists and pedestrians.
livability: Extensive tree planting on both sides and in the median creates a greener and calmer environment than a typical arterial road.
Livability is reduced because the corridor appears dominated by through-movement rather than everyday street life; there are no visible shops, building frontages, or active public destinations.
Very few people are visible, so the image suggests limited social interaction and low street-level activity despite the pleasant greenery.
The right-side path next to the trees may support leisure walking or jogging, adding some recreational value to the corridor.
sustainability: The large number of mature and young trees along both sides and the median contributes to shading, carbon uptake, and improved microclimate.
The landscaped median and planted verges indicate green infrastructure rather than fully hard-paved road edges.
The corridor design appears clean and orderly, with no visible roadside parking encroachment, which can help maintain efficient movement and reduce stop-start conflicts.

Sustainability is weakened somewhat because the visible street space still heavily favors private motor vehicles, while dedicated cycling infrastructure and clear public transport elements are not evident.
aesthetics: The avenue has strong visual coherence through repeated rows of trees, evenly spaced light poles, and a symmetrical road layout.
The road surface, curbs, and planting beds appear well maintained and clean, creating a polished streetscape.
Dense greenery on the right side and the planted median soften the scale of the wide roadway and improve scenic quality.
The long, straight perspective framed by trees gives the street a formal boulevard character with high visual order.
comfort: Thermal comfort is relatively good because continuous tree rows on both sides and in the median provide meaningful shade potential, especially for side paths.
Physical comfort is supported by the smooth asphalt roadway and the visible paved side path, both of which appear even and well maintained.
Psychological comfort benefits from the uncluttered environment, low visible traffic, and generous spacing between travel lanes and the pedestrian corridor.
Comfort is limited by the very wide carriageway and open sun exposure over the central roadway, which may feel hot and less pleasant for users away from the tree canopy.
No benches, shelters, or other resting amenities are visible along the side path, reducing comfort for lingering or longer stays.
walkability: The right-side sidewalk/path appears continuous, separated from moving traffic by a planted verge, which supports basic walking conditions.
Trees along the corridor improve the walking experience through greenery and partial shade.
Walkability is only moderate because the street is very wide and no marked crossings, pedestrian signals, or curb extensions are visible, making cross-street connectivity uncertain.
The corridor lacks visible active edges such as shops, entrances, or public facilities, so walking may be functional or recreational rather than destination-rich.
The long straight road and low pedestrian presence may reduce perceived convenience for short everyday walking trips.
bikeability: Bikeability is weakened because no dedicated bike lane, colored cycle track, or bicycle symbols are visible on the roadway or side path.
The wide, fast-looking multi-lane carriageway may feel uncomfortable for on-road cycling, especially for less confident riders.
Although the right-side path is wide enough to suggest possible shared use, there are no markings confirming legal or safe cycling accommodation.
The planted verge offers some separation from motor traffic if cycling is allowed on the side path, but the absence of clear bicycle infrastructure keeps overall bikeability limited.
